# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical reading: Varga and Holm comment on the Halden pilot

## Overall verdict

The first five sections are a strong piece of re-analysis, and they confirm several problems I suspected from the original paper alone:

- **Attrition:** the organisations that dropped out were not a random group.
- **Hours:** actual hours fell by less than 20%.
- **Revenue:** the 1.4% rise was nominal, and in real terms revenue fell.

The microdata go further than I could. Seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule had started, which the working paper misreported as preparation-phase withdrawals. And in 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher than the index from the organisation's own records. If managers were equally likely to err in either direction, a split that lopsided would happen by chance only about 0.1% of the time.

The comment's conclusion, however, does not follow from its own evidence. It claims the per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact." Its best correction still leaves a gain of +10.8%. The only randomised evidence available, which the comment cites selectively, shows a similar gain. And its novelty argument is not tested, even though the data to test it exist.

## Arithmetic

**Table 2:** all four rows are correct (for example, 95.4 ÷ 0.861 gives +10.8%).

**Real revenue:** 1.014 ÷ 1.041 gives −2.6%, as stated. One caveat: the consumer price index is a rough deflator for business revenue.

**Hours breakdown: this does not add up.** The comment attributes the extra hours to two sources:

- +0.7 hours per day on each of the four remaining days, which is +2.8 hours a week
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the day off

Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours per week. Starting from the 40.3-hour baseline actually worked, it gives about 36.6. The reported pilot figure is 34.6, so roughly two hours are unaccounted for.

- If the breakdown is right, hours fell by only about 9–10%, and the per-hour gain is smaller still.
- If the 34.6 figure is right, the breakdown is wrong.

The comment needs to resolve this either way.

**Novelty extrapolation:** a straight line through the two energy readings (0.61 at month 3, 0.29 at month 6) reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor, but it overstates how long the effect lasts.

## Main problems

### 1. The abstract claims a correction that was never made

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. Attrition is the first of those three. But the 10.8% figure uses the 17 organisations that completed the pilot and had both records and time tracking. It makes no adjustment for the nine that withdrew. Section 6 even calls these "the subset of survivors."

An actual attrition correction would treat withdrawals as failures, or calculate worst-case bounds. That would push the figure lower, but it is not in the paper. As written, the abstract misdescribes the analysis.

### 2. "Entirely an artifact" goes well beyond the evidence

The case for calling the gains entirely an artifact rests on these steps:

- **The comment's own corrections leave about +11%.** The Data Note says this figure describes only a non-random subset, yet the abstract and conclusion generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole.
- **Varden's case-processing offices showed +12.5% output per actual hour** (95% CI 6.9 to 18.4). That result used a randomised control group, administrative output records and timesheet hours. None of the selection, measurement or hours-denominator critiques apply to it. The comment cites Varden's counter offices as "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions the case-processing stratum from the same trial.
- **That leaves novelty as the only explanation for the remaining gain.** As the next section shows, novelty is asserted rather than tested.

### 3. The novelty argument is not tested, though it could be

- The evidence offered is two points of self-reported energy, extended in a straight line. Energy is not output.
- The Halden pilot collected the output index **every month**, and the authors have the microdata. Whether output per hour declined from month to month is the direct test of their hypothesis. They don't report it.
- Saying "the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a rhetorical move, not evidence. The honest conclusion is that durability is unknown.

### 4. The treatment of the meetings hypothesis applies a double standard

- The comment says the Varden meetings analysis was "selected for analysis after the results were known." The Varden paper says the calendar data were collected in **month six**, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The analysis was unregistered, and Varden said so. But the claim that it was chosen after the results is not supported by the Varden paper's own account.
- Varden's authors already flagged the analysis as exploratory, rejected it as evidence of a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test. Saying it "should not be cited as a mechanism" just repeats their own caveat back to them.
- The comment's own novelty account is just as post hoc and has even less data behind it. It gets no equivalent scepticism.
- The meetings explanation does not support the "artifact" conclusion anyway. On the Varden figures, removing 3.3 hours of meetings accounts for most of the per-hour gain. If those meetings were low-value, cutting them is a real efficiency gain. It is just not caused by rest or by short hours as such. That distinction matters a great deal for interpretation, and the comment skips over it.

## Smaller points

- **Record-based output may be biased downward too.** One of the record types used was "billable hours delivered." That measures time spent as much as output, so it falls whenever hours fall. If professional-services firms are well represented among the 23 organisations with records, part of the 3.8-point gap between manager and record indices reflects this, not manager optimism.
- **The retail figure rests on three organisations.** The −11.2% for retail and hospitality comes from the three such organisations with records. That is too few to carry much weight. Its closeness to Varden's −11.4% is suggestive at most: one is a change from the organisations' own baseline, the other is relative to a randomised control group.
- **The data-sharing subsets are self-selected.** The Data Note correctly says that organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the rest. The direction of any bias is unknown; for instance, software firms may be overrepresented.
- **The conclusion's summary is not quite accurate.** It says the remaining gain "coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm." But the decaying measure comes from all employees in all 61 organisations, while the 10.8% comes from 17 of them. The two are not shown to coincide anywhere.

## What the three documents together support

1. **Uncontrolled pilots that use scheduled hours and manager-reported output substantially overstate per-hour gains.** The comment shows this convincingly for the Halden pilot.
2. **Where output depends on staff being present, cutting hours reduces output and worsens service.** The comment's evidence on this point is consistent with Varden's counter offices.
3. **Where output is backlog-based, a gain of roughly 10–12% per actual hour shows up in both the corrected pilot subset and the randomised trial.** Whether it lasts, and how much of it comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest, is not yet known. Varden's 24-month follow-up and its registered meetings test are the right next evidence.

The comment's recommendations for future evaluations are sound:

- record-based output
- actual hours
- a comparison group
- follow-up of at least 18 months
- intention-to-treat analysis that includes organisations that withdraw

Its headline claim that the gains are "entirely an artifact" is not.
